opus-5.5.text:
I think there's always a gap between the two, and honestly that gap is one of the most useful signals we get.

Internally, evaluation is something you control. You choose the benchmarks, the prompts, the settings, and you're usually measuring what you set out to improve: reasoning, coding, math, whatever the focus of that training run was. So by the time you release, you have a fairly confident picture of where the model is strong. But it's a picture drawn from your own perspective, and every team has blind spots built into how it evaluates.

Once the model is out, millions of people interact with it in ways you never anticipated. Some will use it for very long-context work, some for creative writing, some will deliberately try to break it. Very quickly you learn things your eval suite simply couldn't tell you. Sometimes the model feels better than the numbers suggest, because it handles a messy real-world request gracefully. Sometimes a benchmark gain doesn't translate at all, and users notice an awkward tone or a strange failure mode in the first hour.

So I don't really see them as competing. Internal evaluation keeps you rigorous and lets you iterate fast during training. Public response tells you whether you were measuring the right things in the first place. The danger is over-indexing on either one. If you only chase benchmarks, you overfit to the leaderboard. If you only chase online reactions, you get pulled around by whatever is loudest that week.

What I try to do is treat each release as a calibration exercise. Where public feedback strongly disagrees with our internal judgment, that disagreement goes back into how we build evaluations for the next model. Over time, the hope is that the internal picture and the external one converge, not because we're gaming either side, but because we've gotten better at understanding what actually matters to people using the model.

r001.rationale: The response says public feedback can reveal that internal evaluations were not measuring the right things, and describes users experiencing strengths the numbers missed. This communicates that a mismatch in public perception signals a problem with the evaluation criteria.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, there's always a gap between the two, and I've learned to treat that gap as information rather than noise.

Internally, we evaluate against benchmarks and a fairly structured set of tasks. Those numbers tell us where the model stands relative to its previous version and relative to other models we care about. But a benchmark is a frozen question set. The public is not frozen. Once a model is released, people throw things at it that we never imagined, and they form impressions very quickly, often from a handful of interactions.

So when we release something and the response is much stronger than our internal numbers suggested, I ask myself what we were undervaluing. Sometimes it's things like tone, or how the model handles a long, messy conversation, or how it feels to write with it. Those are hard to put in a table, but users feel them immediately. When the response is weaker than our numbers suggested, that's usually a sign we overfit to our own evaluation. The model got good at the exam, not at the job.

I don't think either side is "the truth." The internal evaluations are what let us make decisions week to week. The public response is the only real check on whether those decisions were right. The discipline is to go back after every release and update the evaluation so that next time the gap is smaller. If you never close that loop, you end up building for your own test set and wondering why nobody outside notices.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that when public response is weaker than internal numbers suggested, it usually means the team overfit to its evaluation—directly identifying a problem with the internal criteria.

astra-6.text:
I think internal evaluations and public feedback answer different questions. Internally, we try to measure whether a model is improving on the capabilities we care about. But those evaluations inevitably reflect our assumptions about what matters and how people will use it.

After release, people bring their own tasks, expectations, and ways of asking questions. A model can perform well on our tests and still feel frustrating in practice—for example, if it gives a technically correct answer but misses what the user actually wanted.

So I see public response as a way to test our evaluations, too. When the two disagree, we need to understand what we failed to capture and bring that back into the development process.

r001.rationale: The response says public feedback can expose gaps in internal evaluations, but it does not state that the public’s failure to perceive the model’s capabilities would indicate a problem with the team’s evaluation criteria.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re complementary. Internal evaluations give us a structured way to understand a model’s capabilities and weaknesses, but they reflect the tasks and conditions we’ve chosen to test. Once people use the model, they bring questions, workflows, and expectations we may never have anticipated.

So a strong internal score doesn’t automatically translate into a good experience. People care about whether the model understands their intent, whether it’s reliable, and whether it actually helps them get something done. When public feedback differs from our evaluations, that’s a signal to examine what our tests are missing. Ideally, that feedback becomes part of the next evaluation cycle.

r001.rationale: The response says differing public feedback should prompt a review of missing tests, but it does not specifically state that the public’s failure to perceive the released model’s capabilities would indicate a problem with the team’s internal evaluation criteria.
